html:
Around 825 the Persian scholar al-Khwarizmi, working in Baghdad, wrote a book on calculating with Indian numerals. It spread the decimal place-value system, zero included, through the Islamic world and later to Europe.

The system was Indian. Between the 1st and 4th centuries CE Indian mathematicians worked out how to write any number with ten signs, where a digit's place sets its value. Aryabhata used place value around 499, and Brahmagupta in 628 gave rules for calculating with zero as a number. The Gwalior inscription of 876 shows a written zero in everyday use.

Baghdad, the new capital of the Abbasid Caliphate, was gathering learning from everywhere: Greek science in translation, Persian astronomy, and Indian astronomical tables. Al-Khwarizmi's arithmetic and his book on al-jabr (from which "algebra" comes) made Indian reckoning part of that body of knowledge. The philosopher al-Kindi wrote on Indian numerals soon after.

The numerals then moved west. Latin translations of al-Khwarizmi turned his name into "algorithm". Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202 made the case to Italian merchants, though Roman numerals held on in Europe until printing. The digits most of the world writes today descend from Indian Brahmi numerals, which is why they are often called Hindu-Arabic.
sum: Around 825 the Persian scholar al-Khwarizmi, working in Baghdad, wrote a book on calculating with Indian numerals. It spread the decimal place-value system, zero included, through the Islamic world and later to Europe.
